title: What does BIS expect from export compliance training under the EAR?
description: Element 5 of the BIS Export Compliance Guidelines, how OEE weighs compliance programs in EAR penalties, and who needs training, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Export Administration Regulations (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730 to 774, set no general training mandate, but the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) names training as Element 5 of the eight elements in its Export Compliance Guidelines. Under Supplement No. 1 to 15 CFR Part 766, the Office of Export Enforcement weighs how far a company follows those guidelines when setting penalties, and settlements can require employee training. As at November 2026, training is expected evidence.
keyTakeaways: BIS lists eight elements of an effective Export Compliance Program (ECP): management commitment, risk assessment, export authorization, recordkeeping, training, audits, handling violations and corrective action, and building and maintaining the ECP.

Element 5 says a good training program provides job-specific knowledge, communicates each employee's export responsibilities, and holds employees accountable through assessments, with periodic reviews when products, end users or the EAR change.

Supplement No. 1 to Part 766 makes the "existence, nature and adequacy" of a risk-based compliance program a general factor in penalty decisions, and says OEE will account for how far a respondent follows the Export Compliance Guidelines.
The same supplement allows OEE to require, in a settlement, that the respondent "provide training to employees as part of its compliance program".

Releasing controlled technology or source code to a foreign person in the United States is a deemed export under 15 CFR 734.13(a)(2), so research and engineering staff are part of the training population.
regulator: US Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), including the Office of Export Enforcement (OEE)
appliesTo: Exporters, reexporters and transferors of items subject to the EAR, including dual use commodities, software and technology
Universities, laboratories and companies that release controlled technology or source code to foreign persons in the United States
Freight forwarders and other agents acting for exporters
Defense contractors that also handle Commerce-controlled items alongside ITAR work

sections.heading: Is export compliance training required under the EAR?

blocks.text: The EAR text does not contain a general requirement to train employees or to run an Export Compliance Program. The guidelines themselves list the claim that an Export Compliance Program is not required by the EAR as a common management objection, and answer it with the operational benefits of a program rather than by disputing it. Training is nonetheless built into the way BIS evaluates companies: it is a named element of the [Export Compliance Guidelines](https://www.bis.gov/media/documents/export-compliance-guidelines), and the enforcement guidance in 15 CFR Part 766 uses those guidelines as the measure of a compliance program.

The result is a strong expectation rather than a rule. A company with no training program will find it harder to show the adequacy BIS looks for when a violation is investigated, and a settlement may impose training anyway. Organizations that also handle defense articles should read the separate position under the State Department regime on the [ITAR export compliance training](/regulations/itar-export-compliance-training) page.

sections.heading: What does Element 5 of the Export Compliance Guidelines say?

blocks.text: Element 5 opens with the statement that "a good training program is critical to having an effective compliance program," and asks companies to tailor the message so each staff member understands their role. The guidelines, titled Export Compliance Guidelines: The Elements of an Effective Export Compliance Program and dated January 2017, list three characteristics of a good program.

items: Provides job-specific knowledge based on need.
Communicates the export responsibilities for each employee.
Holds employees accountable for export training through assessments.

blocks.text: The element adds that training should include "periodic reviews and revisions" covering changes in the organization's products and services, end uses or end users, and the EAR itself. It recommends incentives for good compliance behavior "rather than using only scare tactics".

blocks.title: Accountability options BIS describes
blocks.text: Element 5 notes that some companies ask employees to sign a certificate at the end of training accepting responsibility for the content, with disciplinary action for failure to comply, or add training to performance plans. BIS presents these as optional.

sections.heading: What levels of training does BIS recommend?

blocks.text: BIS describes a pyramid of three audiences with increasing depth, and gives a two tier worked example. The tiers are a guide to proportion, not a fixed curriculum.

blocks.text: The example program places an annual training session in the resources for all employees, and BIS seminars or outside programs for the compliance team. BIS does not set a minimum number of hours.

sections.heading: How does training affect EAR penalties?

blocks.text: Training affects penalties through the compliance program factor in BIS enforcement guidance. [Supplement No. 1 to 15 CFR Part 766](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-15/part-766) describes how OEE charges violations and calculates settlement penalties, and Factor F reads: "The existence, nature and adequacy of a Respondent's risk-based BIS compliance program at the time of the apparent violation. OEE will take account of the extent to which a Respondent complies with the principles set forth in BIS's Export Compliance Guidelines."

items: **Remediation questions:** the guidance asks whether the respondent gave the individuals and managers responsible for an apparent violation "additional training" so that similar violations do not recur.

**Settlement terms:** under the heading Training and Audit Requirements, OEE "may require as part of a settlement agreement that the Respondent provide training to employees as part of its compliance program" and submit to internal or independent audits.

**Non-monetary settlements:** for cases that are not egregious, agreements may impose a suspended denial order with conditions "such as training and compliance requirements" instead of a monetary penalty.

**Statutory maximum:** 15 CFR 6.3 lists the inflation-adjusted maximum civil penalty under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 (50 U.S.C. 4819) as $374,474 per violation, as shown in the eCFR as at November 2026.

blocks.text: Voluntary self-disclosure is governed by [15 CFR 764.5](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-15/section-764.5). It allows minor or technical violations without aggravating factors to be bundled into one submission if they occurred within the preceding quarter, which is easier when training and procedure records show the root cause.

sections.heading: Why do research and engineering staff need EAR training?

blocks.text: Because technology can be exported by conversation or file access inside the United States. Under [15 CFR 734.13](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-15/section-734.13), export includes "releasing or otherwise transferring 'technology' or source code (but not object code) to a foreign person in the United States (a 'deemed export')", and paragraph (b) treats that release as an export to the person's most recent country of citizenship or permanent residency.

This is why BIS places technical staff and human resources in the middle tier of its pyramid. A visiting researcher given access to a controlled design repository, or a new hire onboarded to a project without a license check, creates exposure that only trained staff will recognize.

sections.heading: How can a company map EAR training to roles, frequency and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each training need to the BIS element or EAR provision it supports, choose and justify a frequency, and decide in advance what evidence would answer OEE's Factor F questions. The table is illustrative; frequencies are company decisions, because the EAR sets none.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents the BIS elements, the EAR provisions behind them and the company's own procedures as connected nodes, then links each to roles, learning outcomes and assessment points. When an Entity List change or a new rule lands, the affected outcomes and roles are identified before content is rewritten, and the evidence trail answers the compliance program questions in Part 766. More on export control programs for suppliers is on the [government and defense page](/industries/government-defence).

faqs.q: How often should EAR training be repeated?
faqs.a: BIS does not set a frequency. Element 5 calls for a periodic refresher for the general audience and for revisions when products, end users or the EAR change, and its worked example lists annual training. Annual refreshers plus event-driven updates after significant rule changes are a common, defensible choice that the company should document in its ECP manual.

faqs.q: Does BIS certify or approve training programs?
faqs.a: No. BIS publishes guidance, online training and seminars, but it does not approve a company's training program. The adequacy of the program is judged after the fact, for example when OEE weighs Factor F in Supplement No. 1 to Part 766 during an enforcement case.

faqs.q: Is a freight forwarder's training enough for the exporter?
faqs.a: No. The Export Compliance Guidelines state that export control compliance is not a task to outsource to a freight forwarder. Forwarders can advise on logistics, but the exporter remains responsible, so its own staff need training on classification, screening and license determinations.

faqs.q: Should EAR training cover ITAR and sanctions too?
faqs.a: For the export compliance team, yes. Element 5's second tier lists an overview of export regulations from all agencies that affect the company, naming the EAR, ITAR, the Foreign Trade Regulations and OFAC sanctions. General staff usually need only the regime that applies to their work and a clear route for questions.

factCheck.claim: The BIS Export Compliance Guidelines list eight elements, with Training as Element 5; the document is dated January 2017.

Element 5 characteristics: job-specific knowledge based on need, communicates export responsibilities for each employee, holds employees accountable through assessments; periodic reviews for changes in products, end uses or end users, and the EAR.

Element 5 describes a three level pyramid (general audience, positions with export functions, export compliance team) and a two tier example including EAR, ITAR, FTR and OFAC overview for the compliance team.
Supplement No. 1 to Part 766, Factor F: existence, nature and adequacy of a risk-based BIS compliance program; OEE takes account of compliance with the Export Compliance Guidelines.
Supplement No. 1 to Part 766: OEE may require in a settlement agreement that the respondent provide training to employees as part of its compliance program and be subject to audits.
15 CFR 734.13(a)(2) and (b): release of technology or source code to a foreign person in the US is a deemed export to the most recent country of citizenship or permanent residency.
15 CFR 6.3: maximum civil penalty under 50 U.S.C. 4819 adjusted from $364,992 to $374,474.
15 CFR 762.6(a): records required by the EAR must be retained for five years.
15 CFR 764.5: minor or technical violations within the preceding quarter may be bundled into one submission.
The Export Compliance Guidelines list 'An Export Compliance Program is a not required by the EAR' as an example management excuse, answered with the benefits of an ECP.

The Export Compliance Guidelines state export control compliance is not a task that should be outsourced to a freight forwarder, and recommend program level internal audits at least annually (Element 6).
